P1-02.title: Clocks and resets
P1-02.P1: - Clocks and resets. Clock and reset inputs, a reset request the unit only combines, gates, registers or passes to a reset chain or reset output port (its copies and that output port included), and chains only synchronizing or releasing a reset (a reset shift register, a registered reset copy) are not conceptual assets under any question. A serial link's clock line the unit drives to, or senses from, a peer device is not a conceptual asset either, nor is a setting or decision whose only use, apart from a read-back, is to shape that line (polarity, phase against the data, holding it while the peer stretches it), although this rule judges other clock settings as usual. Do not cite their lines as held lines. The link's data and select lines, its rate setting and the unit's clock-enable outputs are judged as usual. A setting's only use is to shape a serial link's clock line also when, apart from its read-back, its counterparts show it gives value to or decides only the element driving that line, and that element gives value to or decides nothing but the line, even where the line's phase sets when the peer samples or sends data. It is then not a piece of its own: keep no concept for it and do not cite its lines as held lines; a transfer-mode, format or rate concept holding other settings stays, without it. Clock-controlling settings or requests (an enable, a rate) are judged as usual, as is a reset-triggering decision (a timeout) where it is computed, not a copy the unit only gates or registers, except as the next sentence says. A decision that a write was refused or carried a wrong value (a write while locked, a wrong password), its gated or registered copies, and a setting choosing only whether such a violation resets are not conceptual assets either when, apart from a read-back, they only request a reset and record its cause, although step 3 makes a compare of a written value with a fixed value a piece. The cause record, the lock refusing the write, and a compare outcome restarting a counter are judged as usual.
P1-02.P2: A setting or decision whose only use, apart from a read-back, is to shape a serial link's clock line that the unit drives to or senses from a peer device (its polarity, its phase against the data, or holding it while the peer stretches it) never qualifies for any conceptual asset: Phase 1 does not keep it as one. Judged as usual: the link's data and select lines, its rate setting (how often the line toggles), an enable, and the unit's clock-enable outputs. A setting's only use is to shape a serial link's clock line also when, apart from its read-back, its counterparts show it gives value to or decides only the element driving that line, and that element gives value to or decides nothing but the line, even where the line's phase sets when the peer samples or sends data. It then never qualifies for any conceptual asset, even a transfer-mode, format or rate concept; it can be a secondary (2.7). A reset request that this unit only combines, gates, registers or passes on to a reset chain or reset output port never qualifies for any conceptual asset, nor do the input port bringing it in, its copies, that output port, or a chain only synchronizing or releasing a reset (a reset shift register): they only carry a decision judged where it is computed. Judged as usual: the record of a reset's cause, a compare outcome that restarts a counter, and, except as the next sentence says, a decision triggering a reset (such as a timeout), where it is computed, not a copy of it that the unit only gates or registers. A decision that a write was refused or carried a wrong value (a write while locked, a wrong password), its gated or registered copies, and a setting choosing only whether such a violation resets never qualify for any conceptual asset if their only uses, apart from a read-back, are to request a reset and record its cause. Judged as usual: the cause record, the lock refusing the write, a compare outcome that restarts a counter, a decision triggering a reset for another cause (such as a timeout) where it is computed, and a refused access raising a trap, a fault or a bus error.

P1-03.title: Build-time values
P1-03.P1: - Build-time values. A generic or constant only fixing the build (a feature switch, size or depth, fixed address or address map, buffering choice) is not a conceptual asset: no element of the IP can change or withhold it at run time. Nor is a run-time bit that a statement ANDs with a build-time switch and whose effect includes writing characters to a file or the screen (a simulation-only mode), although a bus write can change it: it is part of that build choice and is not the run-time decision the next sentence asks for. Instead, name the run-time decision using it as its own concept (which port an address selects, which requester is granted).

P1-04.title: Pacing pulses
P1-04.P1: - Pacing pulses. A tick, edge pulse or divider count made inside the unit only to pace another step, or an input port used only as a condition letting such a tick or count advance, is part of that step or its rate setting (step 3), unless an output port carries the pulse itself (2.2); an output port the pulses only decide or time does not count. Do not name it in any concept's information or cite its lines as held lines. Not pacing pulses: a request held until served, a start pulse decoded from a received command, and a step counter (sequencing state, below, judges a step counter; in a coprocessor, such a count of its busy state is one piece with that state).
P1-04.P2: A tick, edge pulse or divider count made or picked inside the unit only to pace a step (apart from restarting itself, it only makes such a pulse or lets the step advance) is not primary for any conceptual asset unless an output port carries the pulse itself (2.2); a port the pulses only decide or time does not count. It can be a secondary only of a primary whose update it gates (2.7, direction b). Judged as usual: the element storing the rate setting, a request held until served, a start pulse decoded from a received command, a step counter (sequencing state, below, judges it; in a coprocessor, such a count of its busy state is one piece with that state), and a count whose compare with a limit raises a reset, an error or an interrupt, or sets an output level (a timeout or timer count).

P1-05.title: Forwarded transactions
P1-05.P1: - Forwarded transactions. A bus transaction (a request or response with its address, data and handshake) that the unit only forwards between its ports or to a sub-unit, without storing, computing or deciding it, is not a conceptual asset of this unit; this rule, its sentences on relayed data included, never covers a bus whose address this unit drives on a non-record output port of its own and whose acknowledge it takes on a non-record input port of its own (judge from port names which ports are that bus's address, acknowledge and other lines, and say so): the request it drives onto that bus's ports and the response it takes from them are judged as usual, as information leaving and entering the unit there. Also forwarding: merging several ports' bus responses into one (an OR or a multiplexer); a register stage passing a whole request or response record on unchanged a cycle later, although it stores the record; and a record this unit only wires between one of its ports and the port map of an instance of another IP, with no statement of this unit reading or writing it (a constant tied to it in a generate branch lacking the instance is no such statement), even though the black-box rule lets the instance change it. The decision whether or where it passes is judged as usual. Relayed data is data a transfer carries into or out of the unit (data loaded or stored, instruction words fetched, messages received or sent) when no statement of this unit stores it or computes from it: it only moves between a unit port and an instance of another IP, between such instances, or into a statement only mixing it with other values (an OR, a multiplexer). Relayed data, alone or with only the acknowledge and ready lines timing its transfer, is not a piece of its own, even in a unit executing instructions and although step 1 names data received or returned and 4.2 end-user's private data: keep no concept for it. Judged as usual by this rule only: a transfer's address and direction; a wait or fault flag; an interrupt or debug request; a register read-back word, and the register contents an instance holds; an arithmetic, logic or compare result an instance computes from operands; the value a mixing statement writes (such as the value written back to a register); and data the unit stores, shifts through its own register, generates or computes from, even when a buffer instance also holds it. Judge from port names which instance ports carry relayed data and which a computed result, and say so.
P1-05.P2: An internal array whose elements, one per port, this unit sets each to a whole bus request or response record (2.6) copied from one record or a constant, never qualifies for any conceptual asset: it only passes the transaction on, and a select or compare gating an element's strobe only decides that field (2.2) or mixes into it (2.6), so the decision stays where it is computed. A select computed from that compare (such as a bit-per-port vector) is the decision's own element and stays its primary. If the compare is inline in a condition, the decision has no element of its own and adds no primary, even when the held lines assign the array; do not move the primary to the record the array copies or its fields, which only feed the compare or carry the transaction. A single strobe, enable or request flag a decision gates is judged as usual. A record this unit only wires between a unit port and the port map of an instance of another IP, with no statement of this unit reading or writing it or its fields (a constant tied to it in a generate branch lacking the instance is no such statement), never qualifies for any conceptual asset, nor do its fields: the instance holds the value; the record only carries it. Judged as usual: a record this unit's statements read or write, a non-record port even if wired straight into an instance, and an element of this unit deciding whether or where the record passes. Relayed data is data a transfer carries into or out of the unit (data loaded or stored, instruction words fetched, messages received or sent) when no statement of this unit stores it or computes from it: it only moves between a unit port and an instance of another IP, between such instances, or into a statement only mixing it with other values (an OR, a multiplexer). No element qualifies as primary for a conceptual asset about relayed data, alone or with only the acknowledge and ready lines timing its transfer, even in a unit executing instructions and where 4.2 points at it: Phase 1 does not keep such a concept, so it has no secondary (step 5); under other conceptual assets its elements keep their usual labels. Judged as usual: a transfer's address and direction; a wait or fault flag; an interrupt or debug request; a register read-back word, and the register contents an instance holds; an arithmetic, logic or compare result an instance computes; the value a mixing statement writes (such as the value written back to a register); and data the unit stores, shifts through its own register, generates or computes from, even when a buffer instance also holds it. Judge from port names which instance ports carry relayed data and which a computed result, and say so. The relayed-data sentences above never bar a port of a bus whose address this unit drives on a non-record output port of its own and whose acknowledge it takes on a non-record input port of its own (judge from port names which ports are that bus's address, acknowledge and other lines, and say so): judge each such port as usual (2.6, 2.7); under a conceptual asset about what crosses that bus, the relayed-data bar still keeps every other element from being primary, but each can be a secondary of those ports (2.7).

P1-06.title: Second copies
P1-06.P1: - Second copies. An internal register (not a port) that directly copies bits of one other register of its own entity, not as an index, whose other assignments write only constants, and that no condition reads, is a copy kept only while the value moves (2.6). It is not a piece of its own: name its information under the copied register's piece, and do not cite its lines as held lines.
P1-06.P2: An internal register (not a port) that directly copies bits of one other register of its own entity, not as an index, whose other assignments write only constants, and that no condition reads, is a copy kept only while the value moves (2.6). It never qualifies as primary for any conceptual asset: the register it copies keeps its own label, and the copy can be a secondary (2.7, direction a).

P1-07.title: Bus handshake copies
P1-07.P1: - Bus handshake copies. A bus response acknowledge only repeating or delaying the bus request strobe, and a bus error flag tied to a constant, are not information of their own. In a unit passing bus requests from an input bus request port to an output one, a register of one bit, or one bit per requester, not a request waiting for a grant (a rule below), holds no information of its own when every assignment to it (directly or through its next-value signal), apart from clearing or holding it, copies or ORs in only the strobe, lock bit or response error bit of the access in progress, or sets it when a test reading only that access's fields and build-time values holds (a route bit), and the unit reads it only to start, pass on, route, time or end that access, the access it serves or that locked sequence, or to drop words that access fetched: the register only re-times a value the access already carries. It is not a piece of its own, although steps 1 to 4, Build-time values and 4.4 would name it a request, status, lock, select, compare or bypass, and even where another rule judges a decision or held request as usual. A compare or decode reading a register this rule bars, and otherwise only that access's own fields and build-time values, or used only to set such a register, is part of that register (step 3), not a piece of its own. Keep no concept for them and cite none of their lines as held lines, except a line also assigning an element this rule does not bar. Judged as usual: the grant, its select and strobe; an address decode choosing which of several output bus request ports gets the access; a pending fence or flush clearing what the unit stores; a busy flag set when the unit itself issues an access; a timeout count, its error and its suppression flag; a reservation; a software-set lock guarding later accesses; a read enable deciding whether stored data leaves on the response; and a cache's hit. A one-bit register that one unconditional statement sets on every clock edge to a stored state bit or flag of this unit, copied or inverted and ANDed only with terms saying when it applies (a request strobe, its read or write bit, an operation-type decode), and that only a bus response's acknowledge or data fields read, only re-times that state to the response. It is part of that state, not a piece of its own, although step 1 names status and responses and step 3 makes a compare of stored state with a request a piece: keep no concept for it and do not cite its lines as held lines. Judged as usual: that state, where held; a register set only from the unit's input ports (a read enable from a strobe and a read or write bit); and a flag that a condition sets to a constant (a timeout error raised at a count's limit).
P1-07.P2: A one-bit register that one unconditional statement sets on every clock edge to a stored state bit or flag of this unit, copied or inverted and ANDed only with terms saying when it applies (a request strobe, its read or write bit, an operation-type decode), and that only a bus response's acknowledge or data fields read, only re-times that state to the response. It is never primary for any conceptual asset but can be a secondary (2.7). Judged as usual: that state, where held; a register set only from the unit's input ports (a read enable from a strobe and a read or write bit); and a flag that a condition sets to a constant (a timeout error raised at a count's limit). In a unit passing bus requests from an input bus request port to an output one, a register of one bit, or one bit per requester, not a request waiting for a grant (a rule below), holds no information of its own when every assignment to it (directly or through its next-value signal), apart from clearing or holding it, copies or ORs in only the strobe, lock bit or response error bit of the access in progress, or sets it when a test reading only that access's fields and build-time values holds (a route bit), and the unit reads it only to start, pass on, route, time or end that access, the access it serves or that locked sequence, or to drop words that access fetched: the register only re-times a value the access already carries. Such a register and a signal used only to compute its next value never qualify for any conceptual asset: one about such registers alone has no primary, and barring them makes no other element primary instead. They can be secondaries only in direction b (2.7). Judged as usual: the grant, its select and strobe; an address decode choosing which of several output bus request ports gets the access; a pending fence or flush clearing what the unit stores; a busy flag set when the unit itself issues an access; a timeout count, its error and its suppression flag; a reservation; a software-set lock guarding later accesses; a read enable deciding whether stored data leaves on the response; and a cache's hit.

P1-08.title: Working values
P1-08.P1: - Working values. Partial results inside a computation (a partial sum, product or round value, a synchronizer stage, a debiasing step) are part of the result they produce (step 3), not concepts of their own. So are the state and flag made inside a debiasing step to choose which raw bits it accepts: although step 2 would call them a decision, they only shape that result, like a compare picking a minimum (step 3). Do not name a synchronizer stage in any concept's information or cite its lines as held lines.
P1-08.P2: Partial results of a computation of this unit belong to its result and never qualify for any conceptual asset: a partial sum or product, an addend, a subtraction step or round value, a value before the final sign step, a value computed only to be copied, whole or in part, into the finished result's register, a compare only picking that result (a minimum or maximum), and a debiasing step's state and flag choosing which raw bits it accepts. Judged as usual: the element holding the finished result or that an output port takes it from, even while holding operand copies or partial values; a unit port; a signal handed whole to or from an instance; a count; a setting (such as signedness); a serial port's data shift register; and any other decision (such as a compare whose result picks or triggers what happens next, or checks combined per region or entry). A synchronizer stage is not primary for any conceptual asset: a register whose assignments, apart from constants, only copy in one unit input port's bit (directly or through a wire or type conversion only copying it) and shift its own earlier bits along; a wire only copying one of its bits is part of it. Judged as usual: the port itself; a register copying a port with none of its own earlier bits (an input register software reads back); a register whose new bit comes from a stage (a shift register assembling a received word); and an element mixing the port or a stage's bits with other values (a request held until served, a sticky flag).

P1-09.title: Slices
P1-09.P1: - Slices. A signal (not a port) whose only assignment copies part of one element's bits (a slice), or joins signals each doing so from the same element, only carries that element's value (2.2), unless that element is a bus request or response record port or a field of one: such a slice is judged as usual (2.6). Otherwise it is not a piece of its own: do not cite its lines as held lines.
P1-09.P2: A signal (not a port) whose only assignment copies part of one element's bits (a slice), or joins signals each doing so from the same element, only carries that element's value (2.2), unless that element is a bus request or response record port or a field of one: such a slice is judged as usual (2.6). Otherwise it never qualifies as primary for any conceptual asset: the element it takes from keeps its own label, and the signal can be a secondary (2.7, direction a).

P1-10.title: Hand-offs
P1-10.P1: - Hand-offs. Check each port-map line where an instance's non-record output port drives a signal another instance or this unit's logic reads. A wait, fault or write-enable flag, or an access address, that one instance outputs on a non-record port to another instance or this unit's logic is a hand-off; if the RTL cannot show which it is, judge from the port names at either end and say so; a field of a record an instance outputs is never a hand-off, even wired alone into another instance's non-record port. A hand-off is its own piece (step 2), unless Port buffers covers it (then this rule does not apply). No step-3 clause or other rule folds it, even when it travels with the data it qualifies, when another instance outputs the same address earlier or later (cite each output's port-map line, in one piece), or when it is one bit of a count: then hold it at the line assigning that bit to the instance output, and a count kept only to make it belongs to this piece.
P1-10.P2: A wait, fault or write-enable flag, or an access address, that one instance outputs on a non-record port to another instance or this unit's logic is a hand-off; if the RTL cannot show which it is, judge from the port names at either end and say so; a field of a record an instance outputs is never a hand-off, even wired alone into another instance's non-record port. Label a hand-off primary for its conceptual asset where the instance outputs it: the output port of an instance of this file when this unit only wires that port into another instance, and otherwise the unit signal the port map drives; when another instance outputs the same address earlier or later, label each output. When a hand-off is one bit of a count, the line assigning that bit to the output is where it is computed: the count is not primary for that conceptual asset, and can be its secondary (2.7). Apart from the port-buffer bar on a FIFO, no bar in this step covers a hand-off.

P1-11.title: Decided-on instance outputs
P1-11.P1: - Decided-on instance outputs. A value that an instance of this file outputs on a non-record port, other than a hand-off, crosses into this unit whole at the unit signal that port drives through the port map when that signal's closed-set entry gets its value from that instance port and lists "decides" partners, because this unit's decisions then use the value only through that signal (2.6, outward: the instance output this unit then uses as the value itself); when that signal lists no "decides" partner, this sentence does not apply. Hold such a value also at the port-map line wiring that port to that signal (unless the Port buffers rule bars citing that signal's lines), besides any line where the instance computes it; this rule sets only where the piece is held, not whether it is kept.
P1-11.P2: A value that an instance of this file outputs on a non-record port, other than a hand-off, crosses into this unit whole at the unit signal that port drives through the port map when that signal's closed-set entry gets its value from that instance port and lists "decides" partners, because this unit's decisions then use the value only through that signal (2.6, outward: the instance output this unit then uses as the value itself); when that signal lists no "decides" partner, this sentence does not apply. Label that signal primary for its conceptual asset; the instance output port is not primary for it and can be its secondary (2.7, direction a).

P1-12.title: Instance-driven records
P1-12.P1: - Instance-driven records. A record driven whole by one instance of another IP and wired whole into one or more other instances' port maps (decoded controls or fetch results between sub-units; closed set: the record's own entry gets its value from one instance port and gives it only to instance ports) holds nothing of this unit, even if a port map also takes a field alone, a statement of this unit reads one, or it carries the instructions this unit executes: that instance holds each value; the record and its fields, one-bit flags included, only carry copies, and none is a non-record signal. So information such a record or its fields carry, and that no other element except bus request or response record ports stores, computes or passes whole across the boundary (2.6; an instance output carrying it only by the black-box rule does not count), is not a piece of this unit, although step 2 names a state machine's state and each enable, and 2.4 and 4.2 the privilege mode and program counter: keep no concept for it. Information a non-record unit input port itself brings in crosses the boundary whole at that port (2.6), even when the port is wired straight into that instance: list the port under "Enters Through" and hold the information at the line wiring the port. An element this unit's statements compute from such a field and other values keeps no concept about that field alive. Cite no declaration or port-map line of such a record or its fields as a held line. Judged as usual: non-record signals handed between instances; non-record unit ports, even one wired straight into an instance (a debug or interrupt request line); records this unit's statements set, whole or per field; records whose fields port maps or several instances set separately; and, for its other values, an element this unit's statements compute from such a field and other values.
P1-12.P2: A record driven whole by one instance of another IP and wired whole into one or more other instances' port maps (decoded controls or fetch results between sub-units; closed set: the record's own entry gets its value from one instance port and gives it only to instance ports) holds nothing of this unit, even if a port map also takes a field alone, a statement of this unit reads one, or it carries the instructions this unit executes: that instance holds each value; the record and its fields, one-bit flags included, only carry copies, and none is a non-record signal. Such a record and its fields never qualify for any conceptual asset, even where this step's clause on a decision or setting, or 2.6's outward clause or examples, would make one primary; where only these would qualify, the conceptual asset has none. They can be secondaries (2.7). Judged as usual: non-record signals handed between instances; non-record unit ports, even one wired straight into an instance (a debug or interrupt request line); records this unit's statements set, whole or per field; records whose fields port maps or several instances set separately; and, for its other values, an element this unit's statements compute from such a field and other values.

P1-13.title: Register read-back
P1-13.P1: - Register read-back. In a unit executing instructions, the word an instance outputs for reads of its control and status registers, when a statement of this unit merges it directly into the value written back to a register, is its own piece: those registers' contents as software reads them. Hold it at that instance output; no step-3 clause or other rule folds it. In a unit executing instructions, a word that an instance outputs for reads of its own control and status registers, and that this unit reads only in an OR into the word another instance takes in to answer such reads, only carries those registers to the other instance's read-back: the registers (a count, a protection setting, a configuration or status bit) stay inside the first instance, and no statement of this unit stores, computes or decides them (a constant tied to the word in a generate branch lacking that instance is no such statement). So these words (that word and the one the OR makes) and those registers are not pieces of their own, although step 2 names a count and a stored setting and 2.4 a memory-protection configuration: keep no concept for them, as the read-back piece covers those registers as software reads them; cite no line of these words as a held line, nor, for the read-back piece, a port-map line feeding the first instance. Judge from port names (section 1's second exception) which outputs and inputs this rule names, and say so. Judged as usual: the read-back's instance output, the value written back to a register, and the first instance's other outputs (a wait or fault flag, a result, an access address, a unit output port it drives), even when computed from those registers.
P1-13.P2: In a unit executing instructions, a word that an instance outputs for reads of its own control and status registers, and that this unit reads only in an OR into the word another instance takes in to answer such reads, only carries those registers to the other instance's read-back: the registers (a count, a protection setting, a configuration or status bit) stay inside the first instance, and no statement of this unit stores, computes or decides them (a constant tied to the word in a generate branch lacking that instance is no such statement). So these words (that word and the one the OR makes) never qualify for any conceptual asset, even one about those registers; where 2.6 would make only these primary, the conceptual asset has none; they can be secondaries (2.7). For a conceptual asset about the read-back, the other instance's output for such reads, which a statement of this unit merges directly into the value written back to a register, is the primary: the instance output this unit uses as the value itself (2.6, outward), although it carries the first instance's registers only by the black-box rule; 2.6's carrier sentences and this step's bar on what 2.6 says is not primary do not reach it. Judge from port names which instance outputs and inputs these are, and say so. Judged as usual: the value written back to a register, and the first instance's other outputs (a wait or fault flag, a result, an access address, a unit output port it drives), even when computed from those registers.

P1-14.title: Port buffers
P1-14.P1: - Port buffers. A FIFO instance whose write data is a unit input port's value (a bus write, or bits shifted in from a serial input port) only buffers data between two ports. Its fill flags (holds data, has room), push and pop strobes, a command only clearing it, and a flag recording a push while full (even a register of this unit) only time, gate, clear or report on that data: they are not pieces of their own, although step 2 would call some a decision. Judged as usual: the buffered data, an output port these flags decide (an interrupt request, a ready-to-receive line), and a unit enable that also clears the FIFO. A FIFO holding data the unit generates itself (random bits) is not covered: its holds-data flag that a statement of this unit tests to return either that data or something else (the flag withholds the data) and a register whose only use is to clear that FIFO (it discards the data) are each their own piece (step 2) that no step-3 clause folds into that data, the flag held at the line wiring it out of the FIFO, with the read-data line returning the flag as its exit (step 6), and the register held at the line assigning it, while its other flags and its push, pop and enable controls are judged as usual. Any FIFO instance, whatever data it holds, keeps each word only while the word moves (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves), so the signal wired to its write-data input and the signal its read-data output drives only carry the word; the buffered data is judged where the unit generates it (random bits) or where it crosses the unit's boundary. Keep the buffered data as a piece, but cite no line assigning or wiring those two signals as a held line; leave "Held Lines" empty if no other line holds the data. Judge from port names that an instance is a FIFO, which outputs are its flags and which ports carry its data, and say so.
P1-14.P2: If a FIFO instance's write data is a unit input port's value (a bus write, or bits shifted in from a serial input port), the FIFO only buffers data between two ports: its fill flags (holds data or has room), push and pop strobes, a command only clearing it, and a push-while-full flag (even a register of this unit) only time, gate, clear or report on that data and never qualify for any conceptual asset; barring them makes no other element primary instead. Judged as usual: the buffered data, an output port these flags decide (an interrupt request, a ready-to-receive line), a unit enable also clearing the FIFO, and the flags and controls of a FIFO holding data the unit generates (random bits). Any FIFO instance, whatever data it holds, keeps each word only while the word moves (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves), so the signal wired to its write-data input and the signal its read-data output drives only carry the word; the buffered data is judged where the unit generates it (random bits) or where it crosses the unit's boundary. These two signals never qualify as primary for any conceptual asset, even where 2.6's inward or outward clause, or this step's list sparing a signal handed whole to or from an instance, would make them primary; they can be secondaries (2.7, direction a). Judge from port names that an instance is a FIFO, which outputs are its flags and which ports carry its data, and say so.

P1-15.title: Sequencing state
P1-15.P1: - Sequencing state. Outside a coprocessor, a unit shifting in bits it generates, and a test or debug access port that a peer's clock paces, a state machine's state register (not a flag a request or command sets, held until that request is answered; a reservation one access sets and a later one checks; or the current grant, a state naming which requester holds a shared path, with the select and strobe it drives) or a bit, phase, word or step counter (not a count whose compare with a limit raises a reset, error or interrupt, or sets an output level, such as a timeout or timer count, nor that compare's flag or a timeout's suppression flag) that restarts with each transfer or operation the unit performs (even if one bit copies an enable or a queued command picks the first step), and is read only to pick that transfer's next step, to time or gate its strobes, commands, shifts, loads, acknowledges and multiplexers, or to point its address at the next word, is sequencing state: it only orders steps of information other elements hold, so neither it, an internal busy flag decoded from it, nor an internal done flag it sets at its last step is information of its own, while any unit port (even an interrupt request these flags decide), the enable and rate settings, other elements its steps load or drive (a chip-select register, an address), and an instance output port assigned one of its bits (a hand-off when another instance reads it) are judged as usual, and so is a peer's command: when a non-record unit input port (never a clock, a reset or a serial link's clock line) reaches the unit's logic only through synchronizer stages (registers only shifting that port's bit along, and wires only copying one of their bits) that give value to nothing but each other and decide nothing but a state machine's state register, and no conceptual asset holds that state, the port's bit is that peer's command to the state machine, information of its own that enters through that port, whose primary is that port (2.6: the input port setting it), never that state register, which the bit only decides (2.2), nor those stages. Sequencing state and its internal busy and done flags are not pieces of their own, although step 2 names a state machine's state, a count and a select, and 2.4 control flow (a program's): keep no concept for them, and cite none of their lines as held lines, except one also assigning an element this rule does not bar. In a coprocessor, a count that a multi-cycle operation steps every clock cycle of its busy state, and whose end test only leaves that state, is a step counter, one piece of information with that state. Keep that state as a concept and hold the count in it, not in the operation's result or its pacing.
P1-15.P2: Outside a coprocessor, sequencing state (below) is not such a decision or setting. Label a port that step 3 names as setting a state machine's state primary for the conceptual asset about that state; the state register keeps its own label, and synchronizer stages stay barred. Outside a coprocessor, a unit shifting in bits it generates, and a test or debug access port that a peer's clock paces, a state machine's state register (not a flag a request or command sets, held until that request is answered; a reservation one access sets and a later one checks; or the current grant, a state naming which requester holds a shared path, with the select and strobe it drives) or a bit, phase, word or step counter (not a count whose compare with a limit raises a reset, error or interrupt, or sets an output level, such as a timeout or timer count, nor that compare's flag or a timeout's suppression flag) that restarts with each transfer or operation the unit performs (even if one bit copies an enable or a queued command picks the first step), and is read only to pick that transfer's next step, to time or gate its strobes, commands, shifts, loads, acknowledges and multiplexers, or to point its address at the next word, is sequencing state: it only orders steps of information other elements hold, so neither it, an internal busy flag decoded from it, nor an internal done flag it sets at its last step is information of its own, while any unit port (even an interrupt request these flags decide), the enable and rate settings, other elements its steps load or drive (a chip-select register, an address), and an instance output port assigned one of its bits (a hand-off when another instance reads it) are judged as usual, and so is a peer's command: when a non-record unit input port (never a clock, a reset or a serial link's clock line) reaches the unit's logic only through synchronizer stages (registers only shifting that port's bit along, and wires only copying one of their bits) that give value to nothing but each other and decide nothing but a state machine's state register, and no conceptual asset holds that state, the port's bit is that peer's command to the state machine, information of its own that enters through that port, whose primary is that port (2.6: the input port setting it), never that state register, which the bit only decides (2.2), nor those stages. Sequencing state and its internal busy and done flags never qualify for any conceptual asset, even one about that state or a transfer's control flow; where 2.6 would make only these primary, the conceptual asset has none. They can be secondaries only in direction b (2.7). In a coprocessor, a count that a multi-cycle operation steps every clock cycle of its busy state, and whose end test only leaves that state, is a step counter, one piece of information with that state. Label the count primary for that state's conceptual asset, not secondary as a transition input.

P1-16.title: Serial shift registers
P1-16.P1: - Serial shift registers. In a unit shifting data bit by bit onto or off a serial data port, paced by the unit's own rate setting, the data shift register only holds each word while moving it between that port and the element taking or giving the whole word, so the port is where that data crosses the unit's boundary whole (2.6). Keep the data as a piece: list that port under "Enters Through" or "Leaves Through" and cite the lines reading or driving it as entry or exit lines, even when they name the shift register; cite no line assigning the shift register as a held line, and leave "Held Lines" empty if no other line holds the data.
P1-16.P2: A non-record unit port that moves the conceptual asset's value one bit per step crosses the boundary whole, as every bit passes it: the RTL shifts the port's bit into one end of a register carrying that value (2.2), or drives the port from such a register's end bit, even through forwarding wires, synchronizer stages or one-bit registers, and even if the register holds other fields or the port carries other bits at other steps. Label the port primary, not secondary as a path to the register, which keeps its own label. A serial clock line carries no bit of the value, so it is never such a port. In a unit shifting data bit by bit onto or off a serial data port, paced by the unit's own rate setting, the data shift register only holds each word while moving it between that port and the element taking or giving the whole word, so the port is where that data crosses the unit's boundary whole (2.6). That shift register never qualifies as primary for any conceptual asset, even though the serial-port sentence above leaves it its own label and the sentences on partial results and synchronizer stages judge it as usual; it can be a secondary (2.7, direction a).

P1-17.title: Buffer and engine status bits
P1-17.P1: - Buffer and engine status bits. A status bit a bus read returns is not information of its own when every element it copies (even inverted) or combines is barred by this call's rule on a FIFO only buffering data between two ports (never a flag of a FIFO holding data the unit generates itself) or on sequencing state: it only tells software whether the buffered or shifted data can move or was lost, which that data, its settings and the output ports these elements decide already cover. Although step 1 names status and 4.3 status signals, keep no concept for such bits, alone or grouped as the status software reads, and cite no read-data line returning them as a held line. Not covered: a bit returning anything else, even in the same read word (a stored setting, selection or lock, a reset's cause record); it belongs to the piece it returns, as that piece's exit (step 6). Not covered either: the output ports these elements decide (an interrupt request, a ready-to-receive line), a register a test or debug access port shifts out, and, in a unit executing instructions, the word an instance outputs for reads of its control and status registers.
P1-17.P2: A status bit a bus read returns is not information of its own when every element it copies (even inverted) or combines is barred by this call's rule on a FIFO only buffering data between two ports (never a flag of a FIFO holding data the unit generates itself) or on sequencing state: it only tells software whether the buffered or shifted data can move or was lost, which that data, its settings and the output ports these elements decide already cover. The elements such a bit copies or combines stay barred under a conceptual asset about that status; where only they would be primary, it has none. They can be secondaries only as the rule barring them allows (2.7). A bit returning anything else, even in the same read word (a stored setting, selection or lock, the record of a reset's cause), is not covered.

P1-18.title: Port options
P1-18.P1: - Port options. A setting a bus write stores is a port option when, apart from its read-back, its counterparts show it gives value to or decides some element, and each is an interrupt request output (it picks which events raise it), a flow-control handshake output, or an element decided at a test letting a flow-control handshake input (or its synchronized copy) hold a transfer: it only tunes those ports, which carry the outcome. Judge from port names which ports are interrupt requests or flow-control handshakes, never a serial link's clock line, and say so. Judged as usual: those ports, and a setting with another such element (an enable also copied into engine state, clearing a buffer or driving a clock-enable output; a rate setting; a lock; a limit compared with a count). A port option is not a piece of its own, although step 2 names each enable, step 3 splits by use and it gates an output port: keep no concept for it, name it in no concept's information, and cite no line assigning it as a held line. A concept also holding a port it tunes stays, for that port alone.
P1-18.P2: A setting a bus write stores is a port option when, apart from its read-back, its counterparts show it gives value to or decides some element, and each is an interrupt request output (it picks which events raise it), a flow-control handshake output, or an element decided at a test letting a flow-control handshake input (or its synchronized copy) hold a transfer: it only tunes those ports, which carry the outcome. Judge from port names which ports are interrupt requests or flow-control handshakes, never a serial link's clock line, and say so. Judged as usual: those ports, and a setting with another such element (an enable also copied into engine state, clearing a buffer or driving a clock-enable output; a rate setting; a lock; a limit compared with a count). A port option never qualifies for any conceptual asset; where 2.6 would make only port options primary, the conceptual asset has none. It can be a secondary to an output port it tunes (2.7, direction b).

P1-19.title: Cached copies
P1-19.P1: - Cached copies. In a cache (a unit answering a read from its own copy when a stored tag matches the address, else fetching the words over a backing bus), the copied words copy backing-memory data, and the tag and valid bits only record which words are copied: none is a piece of this unit, although steps 1 and 2 would name them and 4.4 names caches. Judged as usual: its decisions (the hit, the bytes a write changes, the address, its fill, clear and invalidate commands, a pending fence or flush), and a memory that is itself the store.
P1-19.P2: In a cache (a unit answering a read from its own copy when a stored tag matches the address, else fetching over a backing bus), the copied words only copy the backing memory, and the tag and valid bits only record which words are copied, so the arrays holding them, and any signal or port only carrying their contents in or out, never qualify for any conceptual asset. Judged as usual: the cache's decisions (the hit, the bytes a write changes, the address, its fill, clear and invalidate commands, a pending fence or flush) and a memory that is itself the store.

P1-20.title: Held addresses
P1-20.P1: - Held addresses. A register whose value, apart from constants and itself, comes only from part of an access's address field, directly or through its next-value wire (a wire giving value to or deciding nothing but that register) or a wire only copying that part, and that only feeds other addresses or indexes a memory, holds that address only while the access is served (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves). It and its next-value wire (not a wire only copying that part and also giving value to or deciding another element: that wire is the address's own element, judged as usual) are part of the access address, not pieces of their own: do not cite their lines as held lines.
P1-20.P2: A register whose value, apart from constants and itself, comes only from part of an access's address field, directly or through its next-value wire (a wire giving value to or deciding nothing but that register) or a wire only copying that part, and that only feeds other addresses or indexes a memory, holds that address only while the access is served (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves). It and its next-value wire (not a wire only copying that part and also giving value to or deciding another element: that wire is the address's own element, judged as usual) never qualify as primary for any conceptual asset, even though the access sets them (2.6); they can be secondaries (2.7, direction a).

P1-21.title: Memory access address
P1-21.P1: - Memory access address. In a unit that is itself the store of a memory (an array it assigns on a clock edge, not a cache's copies), a wire whose only assignment copies or slices the address field of a bus request record port (closed set: role "index", and that field is its only "gets value from" partner) and whose value picks which word of that array an access writes or reads is a select (step 2) deciding which stored word the access uses or changes, so it is a piece of its own, the access address, even though the unit returns it on no output port and holds it in no register, and although Access command fields lists register-select address bits and byte enables, step 3 would merge it into the stored words or the access, and 2.2 calls its use an index flow (that flow carries the address into the word read; it does not make the address only a path to the stored words): a changed address makes the access write or return a word it was not aimed at, so judge its rubric by that mechanism, and hold it at the line assigning it (not its registered copy, which Held addresses bars).

P1-22.title: Operation selectors
P1-22.P1: - Operation selectors. In a unit executing an instruction or atomic memory operation a processor issues to it (a coprocessor, an atomic read-modify-write), instruction or request fields only picking the operation or the result form returned (an opcode, a function code, an instruction-type bit), their stored copies, and flags decoded from them only naming the operation are part of that operation (step 3), not pieces of their own, although step 2 names a select. Do not list them under "Enters Through" or cite their lines as held lines, except a line assigning an element this rule judges as usual. Judged as usual: a start command or pulse, even one decoded per operation (a multiply or divide start), a register access's address and write enable, a completion flag, and a setting decoded from them that changes how operands are read (signedness). A plain bus read or write is not covered: on a record port, Access command fields judges its read or write bit and a read enable made from it. In a unit executing an instruction or atomic memory operation a processor issues to it, a register whose value, apart from constants and itself, comes only from one source operand input (a port or a request-record field) when the operation starts, directly or through its next-value wire, and reaches an output port only through the element holding the result, only holds that operand while the operation uses it (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves). It and its next-value wire are part of that operand's piece: keep that piece, list the operand input under "Enters Through", cite the lines where it takes the operand as entry lines, and do not cite them as held lines.
P1-22.P2: In a unit executing an instruction or atomic memory operation a processor issues to it (a coprocessor, an atomic read-modify-write), instruction or request fields only picking the operation or its result form (an opcode, a function code, an instruction-type bit), their stored copies, and flags decoded from them only naming the operation never qualify for any conceptual asset, being part of the operation they pick, not decisions of their own; they can be secondaries only in direction b (2.7). A flag whose assignment reads more than these fields (a start or valid signal, a state) does not only name the operation. Judged as usual: a start command or pulse, even one decoded per operation (a multiply start, a divide start), a register access's address and write enable, a completion flag, and a setting decoded from these fields (not a copy) changing how operands are read (such as signedness). Not covered: a plain bus read or write; on a record port, the bar above on access command fields judges its read or write bit and a read enable made from it. In a unit executing an instruction or atomic memory operation a processor issues to it, a register whose value, apart from constants and itself, comes only from one source operand input (a port or a request-record field) when the operation starts, directly or through its next-value wire, and reaches an output port only through the element holding the result, only holds that operand while the operation uses it (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves). It and its next-value wire never qualify as primary for any conceptual asset: the operand input keeps its own label; they can be secondaries (2.7).

P1-23.title: Access command fields
P1-23.P1: - Access command fields. On a record port (never on non-record ports, even ones together carrying an access) carrying accesses addressing this unit's own registers, FIFOs, locks or memory words (not a cache's copies), the fields only saying whether an access happens, its direction and which register, FIFO or bytes it reaches (a strobe, a read or write bit, register-select address bits, byte enables; an address indexing a memory's stored words is the access address, not one of them), and a write enable whose assignment reads only these fields and that only lets a register take the written data, are part of the information the access writes or reads, not information of their own. They are not pieces of their own, although steps 1 and 2, Build-time values and Per-region checks would keep some: keep no concept for them; cite no line only testing them, or only assigning such a write enable, as a held line. A signal of its own decoded from these fields that gates or masks what a read returns (a read enable, a select also masking read data), or pops a FIFO of data the unit generates itself, is its own piece (step 2): name it by what it decides and hold it at the line assigning it; no step-3 clause folds it. An inline condition is no such signal, nor is a strobe of a FIFO that Port buffers covers. Such a field whose value a register takes as its new content belongs to that register's piece. Not covered: a request held until served, a select routing it on, and a strobe driven on to a unit output port; an operation's start pulse.
P1-23.P2: On a record port (never on non-record ports, even ones together carrying an access) carrying accesses addressing this unit's own registers, FIFOs, locks or memory words (not a cache's copies), the fields only saying whether an access happens, its direction and which register, FIFO or bytes it reaches (a strobe, a read or write bit, register-select address bits, byte enables; an address indexing a memory's stored words is the access address, not one of them), and a write enable whose assignment reads only these fields and that only lets a register take the written data, are part of the information the access writes or reads, not information of their own. They never qualify for any conceptual asset, whether or not the port is a bus request or response record, and can be secondaries (2.7, direction b) of the element the access writes, reads or decides. Judged as usual: a separate signal decoded from these fields that gates or masks what a read returns or pops a FIFO of data the unit generates itself (the decision's own element), a register loaded with such a field's value, a request held until served, a select routing it on, a strobe driven on to a unit output port, and an operation's start pulse.

P1-24.title: Per-region checks
P1-24.P1: - Per-region checks. When the unit makes the same compare or permission check per region or entry and only combines the results (a priority chain, an OR) into one decision, that decision is the piece, held where they combine; the per-region results are its working values (step 3), although step 3 makes a compare of stored state with a request a piece. A per-entry result itself picking where a request goes or which entry an access changes (which port an address selects, which lock is addressed) stays its own piece.

P1-25.title: Arbitration bookkeeping
P1-25.P1: - Arbitration bookkeeping. A register only remembering the previous grant for round-robin priority (not the current grant, its select and strobe, or a request held until served) holds no decision of its own: it only tilts the next grant. It is not a piece of its own, although step 2 names a select: keep no concept for it, nor cite its lines as held lines.
P1-25.P2: A register only remembering the previous grant for round-robin priority (not the current grant, its select and strobe, or a request held until served) holds no decision of its own: it only tilts the next grant. It, and a signal used only to compute its next value, never qualify for any conceptual asset; it can be a secondary only to the primaries of the grant reading it (2.7, direction b).

P1-26.title: Requests waiting for a grant
P1-26.P1: - Requests waiting for a grant. In a unit with a test choosing which of several requesters an output bus request port serves (it reads each requester's request strobe and assigns which one holds that port), a one-bit register per requester whose assignments, apart from reset and clearing it while that requester holds the port, only OR in that requester's request strobe, and that this test reads, stores a request taken and not yet served; the signal the grant's statements set that drives that port's strobe field decides whether an access passes on, not who holds the port: each is information of its own, apart from the grant, which the state register naming the holder and the select hold; this rule does not cover lock bits copied from the requests' lock fields or a register only remembering the previous grant. Step 3's timing clause and the rules on bus handshake copies, arbitration bookkeeping, sequencing state and pacing pulses do not cover such a register or that strobe signal: keep the waiting requests as one piece and the strobe signal as another, each apart from the grant, and cite every line assigning them as held lines, reset lines included.

P1-27.title: Processor context fields
P1-27.P1: - Processor context fields. A field, of a record input port other than a bus request or response record port (2.6), that tells the processor's privilege mode, whether it is in debug mode or takes a trap, or whether the current access is a fetch or data access, read or write, only refines a decision this unit computes from other information when this unit only tests it (a condition, select, compare with a fixed value, gate on another result), directly or through a wire only selecting between such fields: the processor holds that state; the record carries a copy. Such a field or wire is part of the decision it refines (step 3), not a piece of its own, although steps 1 and 2 would name it and 2.4, 4.2 and 4.4 point at privilege and debug modes: keep no concept for it, nor list it under "Enters Through" or cite its lines as held lines, except a line assigning an element this rule judges as usual. Judged as usual: the decision such a field refines, where computed or stored (a permission verdict, fault output, execution state); the access address, compared with stored state; and the address, write enable and data of a write to a register of this unit. Not covered: the whole record port, a non-record input port (a peer's flow-control line, an interrupt or debug request), and a port or field wired into an instance. Judge what a field tells from port field names and their uses; say so.
P1-27.P2: A field, of a record input port other than a bus request or response record port (2.6), that tells the processor's privilege mode, whether it is in debug mode or takes a trap, or whether the current access is a fetch or data access, read or write, only refines a decision this unit computes from other information when this unit only tests it (a condition, select, compare with a fixed value, gate on another result), directly or through a wire only selecting between such fields: the processor holds that state; the record carries a copy. Such fields and wires never qualify for any conceptual asset; where 2.6 would make only these primary, the conceptual asset has none. They can be secondaries only in direction b (2.7). Judged as usual: the decision such a field refines, where computed or stored (a permission verdict, fault output, execution state); the access address, compared with stored state; and the address, write enable and data of a write to a register of this unit. Not covered: the whole record port, a non-record input port (a peer's flow-control line, an interrupt or debug request), and a port or field wired into an instance. Judge what a field tells from port field names and their uses; say so.

P2X-decode-output-port-of-a-stored-selec.title: P2-only: decode output port of a stored selection
P2X-decode-output-port-of-a-stored-selec.P2: An output port set only from a stored selection, one line per value (a decode), returns it unmixed: label it primary for that selection.

P2X-unmixed-copy-output-port.title: P2-only: unmixed-copy output port
P2X-unmixed-copy-output-port.P2: A non-record output port (not a serial clock line), of the unit or of an entity of this file the unit instantiates, whose only assignment is one concurrent statement copying unchanged a whole element (no index or slice) that this walk labels primary, returns that element unmixed (2.6), also for a setting, and even where the unit wires the port into a FIFO's write-data input, as the FIFO sentence below bars the unit's signal on that input, not the port driving it, and except an instance's port whose port-map signal in this unit gets its value from that port and lists "decides" partners (that signal is primary instead, by the sentence on a value an instance of this file outputs, or, for a hand-off, by the sentences on hand-offs): label the port primary, not secondary as a path to that element, which keeps its own label.

P2X-input-port-setting-the-value.title: P2-only: input port setting the value
P2X-input-port-setting-the-value.P2: A non-record unit input port (not a clock, a reset, a reset request, a serial clock line, or a port whose bits only become ticks pacing a step) that the RTL copies unchanged into the conceptual asset's value, alone or side by side with other such ports, or reduces to one bit that alone, apart from constants, sets the register holding the conceptual asset (the input port setting it, 2.6), or wires straight into an instance input taking that value, crosses the boundary whole: label it primary for that conceptual asset, not secondary as a path to or a decider of an element computed from it, which keeps its own label; this sentence only adds primaries, so a port it does not cover (such as one the RTL only tests, or reduces to one bit it then mixes with other values) is labelled as if this sentence were absent.

P2X-side-by-side-port-signal-into-instan.title: P2-only: side-by-side port signal into instance
P2X-side-by-side-port-signal-into-instan.P2: Placing such ports side by side combines no per-region results (2.6), and a signal doing only that and wired whole into an instance input is the inward signal of 2.6, not a forwarding wire: label it primary too.

P2X-bus-request-response-record-port.title: P2-only: bus request/response record port
P2X-bus-request-response-record-port.P2: A bus request or response record port, or any field of one, never qualifies (2.6), even as the conceptual asset's only entry or exit port.

P2X-rom-lookup-element.title: P2-only: ROM lookup element
P2X-rom-lookup-element.P2: When a bus read returns, unchanged, words that some build (one generate branch) holds only in a ROM (no element, section 1), the element the ROM lookup writes in that build is where they are stored or computed in this unit (2.6), not a carrier, as no earlier element holds them: label it primary for their conceptual asset, even where another build only passes a stored word through it (each pair gets one label). A bus response field the lookup writes directly still never qualifies.

P2X-other-2-6-non-primaries.title: P2-only: other 2.6 non-primaries
P2X-other-2-6-non-primaries.P2: Any other element that 2.6 says is not primary never qualifies either, even where this step's clause on a decision or setting would make it one.

P2X-count-started-flag.title: P2-only: count-started flag
P2X-count-started-flag.P2: A register only recording that a count has started, read only to let that count advance or to qualify a compare on it, is not primary for any conceptual asset: it decides the count but never carries it (2.2). It can be a secondary only in direction b (2.7). Judged as usual: the compare's result, a flag a request or command sets until served (busy or pending), a start or clear pulse decoded from a command, a timeout's suppression flag, and a completion flag.

P2X-constants-only-instance-control-wire.title: P2-only: constants-only instance control wire
P2X-constants-only-instance-control-wire.P2: A constants-only wire this unit wires into an instance input, decided only by this unit's registers, one holding a command or setting a bus write stores (such as a wire asserted while a stored clear command is set or a stored enable is off), makes its own decision for that instance and holds no command or setting (2.2). It never qualifies as primary for a conceptual asset about such a command or setting; the register holding it keeps that primary, and the wire can be a secondary (2.7).

P1-22R.title: Operation selectors (revised scope)
P1-22R.P1: - Operation selectors. Instruction or request fields only picking an operation or the result form returned (an opcode, a function code, an instruction-type bit), their stored copies (a register taking the value of such a field, or of a code below, unchanged, whatever test picks when it loads), and flags or codes decoded from these fields only naming the operation (one also made from a start, a valid signal or a state does not only name it) are part of the operation they pick (step 3), not pieces of their own, although step 2 names a select, in these units only: a unit executing an instruction or atomic memory operation a processor issues to it (a coprocessor, an atomic read-modify-write), even when it decodes those fields further, accepts or refuses the instruction, starts its own internal units or steps through states; and a unit turning an atomic memory instruction a processor issues to it into a bus access carrying the operation's code to the unit executing that operation (a unit performing a processor's loads and stores), for that instruction only, where these fields and codes, even those also deciding a bus lock held while the operation lasts, are part of that access's piece; but never the unit holding each whole instruction word in a register of its own and issuing its operations to the units executing them (the processor's control unit, not covered, even for the codes and commands it makes from an instruction for those units). Do not list these fields, copies, flags or codes under "Enters Through" or cite their lines as held lines, except a line assigning an element this rule judges as usual. Judged as usual: a start command or pulse, even one decoded per operation (a multiply or divide start), a register access's address and write enable, a completion flag, and a setting decoded from these fields (not a copy) that changes how operands are read (signedness). A plain read or write is not covered, whether a unit answers it on a bus or issues it for a load or store instruction, nor are the fields picking its direction, its size or how the word read is extended; for one the unit answers on a record port carrying accesses to its own registers, FIFOs, locks or memory words, Access command fields judges its read or write bit and a read enable made from it. In a unit executing an instruction or atomic memory operation a processor issues to it, a register whose value, apart from constants and itself, comes only from one source operand input (a port or a request-record field) when the operation starts, directly or through its next-value wire, and reaches an output port only through the element holding the result, only holds that operand while the operation uses it (2.6: a copy kept only while the value moves). It and its next-value wire are part of that operand's piece: keep that piece, list the operand input under "Enters Through", cite the lines where it takes the operand as entry lines, and do not cite them as held lines.
P1-22R.P2: Instruction or request fields only picking an operation or the result form returned (an opcode, a function code, an instruction-type bit), their stored copies (a register taking the value of such a field, or of a code below, unchanged, whatever test picks when it loads), and flags or codes decoded from these fields only naming the operation (one also made from a start, a valid signal or a state does not only name it) never qualify for any conceptual asset, being part of the operation they pick, not decisions of their own, in these units only: a unit executing an instruction or atomic memory operation a processor issues to it (a coprocessor, an atomic read-modify-write), even when it decodes those fields further, accepts or refuses the instruction, starts its own internal units or steps through states; and a unit turning an atomic memory instruction a processor issues to it into a bus access carrying the operation's code to the unit executing that operation (a unit performing a processor's loads and stores), for that instruction only, where these fields and codes, even those also deciding a bus lock held while the operation lasts, are part of that access; but never the unit holding each whole instruction word in a register of its own and issuing its operations to the units executing them (the processor's control unit, not covered, even for the codes and commands it makes from an instruction for those units). These fields, copies, flags and codes can be secondaries only in direction b (2.7). Judged as usual: a start command or pulse, even one decoded per operation (a multiply start, a divide start), a register access's address and write enable, a completion flag, and a setting decoded from these fields (not a copy) changing how operands are read (such as signedness). Not covered: a plain read or write, whether a unit answers it on a bus or issues it for a load or store instruction, and the fields picking its direction, its size or how the word read is extended; for one the unit answers on a record port carrying accesses to its own registers, FIFOs, locks or memory words, the bar above on access command fields judges its read or write bit and a read enable made from it.
